newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-ATHERTON LIKELY TO EXTEND TENURE AS ENGLAND CAPTAIN.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-ATHERTON LIKELY TO EXTEND TENURE AS ENGLAND CAPTAIN.

text.p: Mike Atherton embellished his place in the history books, probably extended his tenure as England captain and won a glowing endorsement from a former Australian test cricketer during a day of personal triumph on Tuesday.

The obdurate Lancastrian, seemingly unable to put bat to ball during the Zimbabwe leg of the tour, added 118 to his unbeaten first innings 94 as England defeated New Zealand by four wickets at Lancaster Park in Christchurch to win the three-test series 2-0.
New Zealand coach Steve Rixon, who kept wicket in 10 tests for Australia in the late 1970s, believed Atherton was the difference between the teams in a fluctuating match.
Rixon was also in no doubt that Atherton was the right man to lead England against Australia in this summer's six-test Ashes series.
"I'd give him anything he wants tonight," Rixon said. "The way he went about the job was a personal inspiration."
England assistant coach John Emburey endorsed Rixon's comments.
"He's got to captain the side against Australia," he said. "He's played against Australia and been on the losing side before. I'm sure he'd like to be a winning captain against them."

Atherton, pilloried in some sections of the British media after England failed to win either test in Zimbabwe as well as failing dismally in the one-day series, treated success as impassively as failure.

Preferring to talk about the side's performance rather than his own, Atherton said the winter campaign had been important "to try and get a settled side and to try and get the right balance to our side and to try and get confidence and winning."
And he said he did not envisage changes for the side to meet the supremely confident Australians, who have held the Ashes since 1989.
"I can't see the side being too different from the one that has just won back-to-back test matches," he said.

Atherton has his critics as captain, although his modest record since taking over from Graham Gooch in 1993 has more to do with a shortage of test class strike bowlers than any inherent tactical weaknesses.
There can be no doubt, though, about his calibre as an opening batsman.

Despite coping with the pressures of captaincy and the knowledge that he is the prime target for opposing bowlers, Atherton has increased his test average from the late 30s to just over 40 and played a series of memorable rearguard actions.

The only other England side to score more than 300 to win a test match featured the most famous opening pair of them all in Jack Hobbs and Herbert Sutcliffe, who laid the foundation for victory over Australia at Melbourne in 1929 with a century partnership on a treacherous pitch.

Whatever his fate against the old enemy this year, Atherton is a worthy successor to Hobbs, Sutcliffe, Len Hutton and Geoff Boycott as a skilled and obstinate technician who has never sold his wicket cheaply.
